citation.title: Research Note: A More Powerful Test Statistic for Reasoning about Interference between Units

standing_assumptions:
The work is a nine-page research note (Political Analysis (2016) 24:395–403; printed page = PDF page + 394, so printed p. 395 is PDF p. 1). It states no theorem, proposition, lemma or proof. Its mathematics is the randomization-test procedure of Section 1, the Kolmogorov–Smirnov formula of footnote 3, the three numbered displays (1)–(3) and the unnumbered application model of Section 3; everything else is simulation and one application. Everything quoted below was read from the page images (the staged 110-dpi images, and 200- and 400-dpi renderings of the staged PDF for subscripts and footnotes).
(S1) Outcomes under interference. p. 395 (PDF p. 1), Section 1: “In a randomized experiment with $n = 4$ subjects connected via a fixed network, the response of subject $i = 1$ might depend on the different ways that treatment is assigned to the whole network. When the treatment assignment vector, $\mathbf{z}$, provides treatment to persons 2 and 3, $\mathbf{z} = \{0, 1, 1, 0\}$, person $i = 1$ might respond one way, $y_{i=1,\mathbf{z}=\{0,1,1,0\}}$, and when treatment is assigned to persons 3 and 4, $\mathbf{z} = \{0, 0, 1, 1\}$ person $i = 1$ might act another way, $y_{i=1,\mathbf{z}=\{0,0,1,1\}}$. More generally, we might say that if the experiment had a causal effect on person $i$, then her outcome would differ under different realizations of the experimental treatment as a whole $y_{i,\mathbf{z}} \neq y_{i,\mathbf{z}'}$.” Footnote 1 (p. 395): “In simpler settings, where treatment given to one individual has no effect on any other individual, we tend to write $y_{i,Z_i=1} \neq y_{i,Z_i=0}$ to say that treatment had a causal effect on person $i$.”
(S2) The testing procedure. p. 396 (PDF p. 2), Section 1: “Say $Y_i$ is the observed outcome, and we hypothesize that units do not interfere and also that $y_{i,Z_i=1} = y_{i,Z_i=0} + \tau$. We can assess which (if any) hypothesized values of $\tau$ appear implausible from the perspective of the data by: (1) mapping the hypothesis about unobserved quantities to observed data using the identity $Y_i = Z_i y_{i,Z_i=1} + (1 - Z_i) y_{i,Z_i=0}$—noticing that if $y_{i,Z_i=1} = y_{i,Z_i=0} + \tau$ then $y_{i,Z_i=0} = Y_i - Z_i\tau$ (by substituting from the hypothesized relationship into the observed data identity); (2) using this result to adjust the observed outcome to represent what would be implied by the hypothesis for a given $\tau_0$ such that $\tilde y_{i,Z_i=0} = Y_i - Z_i\tau_0$; and (3) under the hypothesis, $\tilde y_{i,Z_i=0}$ should have no systematic relationship with treatment assignment, so we can summarize this relationship with a test statistic, $\mathcal{T}(\tilde y_{i,Z_i=0}, Z_i)$. A distribution of values for this test statistic arises from repetitions of the treatment assignment process (new draws of $\mathbf{z}$ from all of the ways that such treatment assignment vectors could have been produced); and finally (4) a $p$ value arises by comparing the observed test statistic, $\mathcal{T}(Y_i, Z_i)$ against the distribution of that test statistic that characterizes the hypothesis.” The paper gives no formula for the $p$ value and does not say which tail (or tails) of the reference distribution is used.
(S3) The KS statistic. Footnote 3, p. 396 (PDF p. 2): “If the empirical cumulative distribution function (ECDF) of the treated units is $F_1$ and the ECDF of the control units is $F_0$, then the KS test statistic is $\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{y}_0, \mathbf{z})_{\mathrm{KS}} = \max_{i=1,\ldots,n}\left[F_1(y_{i,0}) - F_0(y_{i,0})\right]$, where $F(x) = (1/n)\sum_{i=1}^{n} I(x_i \le x)$ records the proportion of the distribution of $x$ at or below $x_i$ (Hollander 1999, section 5.4).”
(S4) Validity as the paper states it. p. 397 (PDF p. 3): “Such results mean that a test of the sharp null of no effects based on a known randomization using any effect increasing test statistic ought to be a valid test (in that the test should produce $p$ values less than $\alpha$ no more than $100\alpha\%$ of the time when the null is true) even though different test statistics may imply different power against false hypotheses.”
(S5) The simple SSR statistic and the no-interference simulation. p. 397 (PDF p. 3), Section 2: “For example, the implication of the constant, additive effects model, $\tilde y_{i,Z_i=0} = Y_i - Z_i\tau$, only changes the distribution of outcomes for units in the treated condition.” Equation (1), with the sentence that introduces it: “The simplest version of the sum-of-squared-residual (SSR) test statistic merely sums the difference between the mean of the outcome implied by the hypothesis and individual outcomes, thereby including the correlation between treated and control outcomes as a part of the distribution of the statistic: $$\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{y}_0, \mathbf{z})_{\mathrm{SSR}} \equiv \sum_i \left(\tilde y_{i,Z_i=0} - \bar{\tilde y}_{i,Z_i=0}\right)^2 \quad (1)$$” Design: “we created a small simulation study of 256 units with half assigned to a binary treatment completely at random. We compared the performance of the two test statistics on two outcomes with no interference—a Normal outcome and a skewed outcome, both with mean of 10 and standard deviation of 1, as shown in Fig. 1.” Models: “We compared two models of effects—a constant additive effects model in which $y_{i,Z_i=1} = y_{i,Z_i=0} + \tau$ and a constant multiplicative effects model in which $y_{i,Z_i=1} = y_{i,Z_i=0} \cdot \tau$. We set the truth to be the sharp null of no effects such that the true $\tau = 0$ for the additive model and the true $\tau = 1$ for the multiplicative model.”
(S6) The SSR statistic with network information. p. 399 (PDF p. 5), Section 2.1: “In the case where we know the fixed binary adjacency matrix of a social network, $\mathbf{S}$, where a given entry in the $n \times n$ matrix is 1 if two units are adjacent and 0 if two units are not adjacent, and where we imagine that network attributes (like degree) of a node play a role in the mechanism by which treatment propagates, the idea of assessing model fit rather than closeness of distributions leads naturally to the SSRs from a least squares regression of $\tilde y_{i,Z_i=0}$ on $Z_i$ and $\mathbf{z}^T\mathbf{S}$ (i.e., the number of directly connected nodes assigned treatment) as well as the $\mathbf{1}^T\mathbf{S}$ (i.e., the degree of the node). If we collected $Z_i$, $\mathbf{z}^T\mathbf{S}$, and $\mathbf{1}^T\mathbf{S}$ into a matrix $\mathbf{X}$, and fit the $\tilde y_{i,Z_i=0}$ as a linear function of $\mathbf{X}$ with fitted coefficients $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ then we could define the test statistic as $$\mathcal{T}(y_0, \mathbf{z})_{\mathrm{SSR}} \equiv \sum_i \left(\tilde y_{i,Z_i=0} - \mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\right)^2. \quad (2)$$” (In display (2) the first argument is printed as an italic $y_0$; in display (1) and in footnote 3 it is a bold $\mathbf{y}_0$.)
(S7) The network model, design and tests. p. 399 (PDF p. 5), Section 2.2: “Their model of treatment propagation was $$\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{z}}, \mathbf{w}, \beta, \tau) = \frac{\beta + (1 - w_i)(1 - \beta)\exp(-\tau^2\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{S})}{\beta + (1 - z_i)(1 - \beta)\exp(-\tau^2\mathbf{z}^T\mathbf{S})}\,\mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{z}}. \quad (3)$$ Briefly, this model posits that treatment effects can depend on either direct assignment to treatment ($\mathbf{z}$) governed by $\beta$ or spillover as an increasing (but flattening) function of the number of directly connected treated neighbors ($\mathbf{z}^T\mathbf{S}$) and is governed by $\tau$. So, we have a model with two parameters. The network used by BFP involves 256 nodes connected in an undirected, random graph with node degree ranging from 0 to 10 (mean degree 4, 95% of nodes with degree between 1 and 8, five unconnected nodes with degree 0). Treatment is assigned to 50% of the nodes completely at random in the BFP example.” pp. 399–400 (PDF pp. 5–6): “We assess three versions of the SSR test statistic versus three versions of the KS test statistic. The first, described above, we call the SSR + Design test statistic because it represents information about how treatment is assigned to the nodes, $\mathbf{z}^T\mathbf{S}$. The second version of the SSR test statistic (SSR + Degree) only includes network degree, $\mathbf{1}^T\mathbf{S}$, and excludes information about the treatment status of other nodes. And the third version (SSR) includes only treatment assignment $\mathbf{z}$.” p. 400: “For each test statistic, we tested the hypothesis $\tau = \tau_0, \beta = \tau_0$ by using a simulated permutation test: we sampled 1000 permutations. We executed that test 10,000 times for each pair of parameters. The proportion of $p$ values from that test less than .05 is plotted in Fig. 3: darker values show fewer rejections, lighter values record more rejections.” p. 400: “The KS + Design and KS + Degree panels show the power of applying the KS test to residuals from linear models including network degree only (the + Degree version) or degree and also the number of treated neighbors (the +Design version).” Fig. 3 caption, p. 401 (PDF p. 7): “Proportion of $p$ values less than .05 for tests of joint hypotheses about $\tau$ and $\beta$ for the model in equation (3). Darker values mean rare rejection. White means rejection always. Truth is shown at the intersection of the straight lines $\tau = .5, \beta = 2$. Each panel shows a different test statistic. The SSR tests refer to equation (2), the KS tests refer to the expression in footnote 3.”
(S8) The application model. p. 400 (PDF p. 6), Section 3: “Coppock reanalyzes the experimental results with an eye toward spillover, constructing a social network based on similarity on W-NOMINATE ideology scores. Coppock hypothesized that ideologically similar legislators would be more likely to share information.” “With distance matrix $\Gamma$, Coppock evaluated the model: $$\mathbf{y}_0 = \mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{z}} - \beta_1\mathbf{z} - \beta_2 g(\Gamma\mathbf{z}),$$ where $g$ is a function that normalizes the sums of distances to treated neighbors to have unit variance. This model has a direct effect ($\beta_1$) and an indirect effect ($\beta_2$) that is linear in the distances to treated neighbors. Coppock evaluated this spillover model using the SSR + Design statistic as presented in this article.”
(S9) Conventions of this list (not the paper's notation). In the targets, $u \in \mathbb{R}^n$ (or $a$) is the vector of hypothesis-adjusted outcomes $u_i = \tilde y_{i,Z_i=0}$, held fixed while the assignment is redrawn; $z \in \{0,1\}^n$ is an assignment with $n_g = \#\{i : z_i = g\}$ units in group $g$ ($g = 1$ treated, $g = 0$ control); $\bar u_g$ or $m_g$ is the mean of $u$ over group $g$; $R(u,z) = \sum_i (u_i - \bar u_{z_i})^2$ is the residual sum of squares from the least-squares regression of $u$ on an intercept and $z$ (the statistic that the paper calls ‘SSR’, as the released code computes it); $F_g(t) = n_g^{-1}\#\{i : z_i = g,\ u_i \le t\}$ and $D(u,z) = \max_i |F_1(u_i) - F_0(u_i)|$ is the two-sided KS distance (as the released code computes it). The expressions $\mathbf{z}^T\mathbf{S}$ and $\mathbf{1}^T\mathbf{S}$ in displays (2) and (3) are read componentwise: for unit $i$, $(z^TS)_i = \sum_j z_j S_{ji}$ (the number of treated neighbours) and $(1^TS)_i = \sum_j S_{ji}$ (the degree). A randomization design is a probability distribution on a finite set $\Omega \subseteq \{0,1\}^n$ of assignments; ‘completely at random’ with half treated is read as the uniform distribution on the assignments with exactly $n/2$ treated units. Witnesses and corrected statements are the validators' and Sol's constructions unless a passage is marked as printed.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 1, step (4) of the testing procedure, corrected: the observed statistic is $\mathcal{T}(\tilde y_{i,Z_i=0}, Z_i)$ at the realized assignment
canonical_claim.location: p. 396 (PDF p. 2), Section 1, second full paragraph, step (4)
canonical_claim.statement:
Sol's repair (validated.json, P016-E001, smallest_repair), verbatim: “In step (4), replace $\mathcal{T}(Y_i,Z_i)$ with $\mathcal{T}(\tilde y_{i,Z_i=0},Z_i)$, evaluated at the realized assignment.” Sol's corrected text (prior_correction.corrected_text), verbatim: “Let $u_i=Y_i-\tau_0Z_i$. Compare the observed $T(u,Z)$ with the distribution of $T(u,Z')$, where $Z'$ follows the experimental assignment law and $u$ is held fixed.”
Corrected step (4): “(4) a $p$ value arises by comparing the observed test statistic, $\mathcal{T}(\tilde y_{i,Z_i=0}, Z_i)$ against the distribution of that test statistic that characterizes the hypothesis.”
Mathematical content, with every hypothesis. Let $\Omega \subseteq \{0,1\}^n$ be finite, $P$ a probability distribution on $\Omega$, and $Z \sim P$. Let $y_{\cdot,0} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $\tau \in \mathbb{R}$ be fixed, with no interference and $y_{i,1} = y_{i,0} + \tau$, so that $Y_i = Z_i y_{i,1} + (1 - Z_i) y_{i,0} = y_{i,0} + \tau Z_i$. For $\tau_0 \in \mathbb{R}$ put $u_i(\tau_0) = Y_i - \tau_0 Z_i$.
(a) $u_i(\tau_0) = y_{i,0} + (\tau - \tau_0) Z_i$ for every $i$; in particular, if the hypothesis is true ($\tau_0 = \tau$), then $u(\tau_0) = y_{\cdot,0}$ for every realization of $Z$.
(b) Hence, if $\tau_0 = \tau$, then for every function $\mathcal{T} : \mathbb{R}^n \times \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ the observed statistic $\mathcal{T}(u(\tau_0), Z)$ has exactly the distribution of the reference statistic $\mathcal{T}(u, Z')$ computed with $u = u(\tau_0)$ held fixed and $Z' \sim P$; and the $p$ value $p = \Pr_{Z'}\{\mathcal{T}(u,Z') \ge \mathcal{T}(u,Z)\}$ satisfies $\Pr\{p \le \alpha\} \le \alpha$ for every $\alpha \in [0,1]$ (the general statement is P016-T12 (iii)).
(c) [Why the printed argument is not the intended one] For the difference in group means $\mathcal{T}(v,z) = \bar v_{z=1} - \bar v_{z=0}$ and every $z$ with both groups non-empty, $\mathcal{T}(Y,z) = \mathcal{T}(u(\tau_0), z) + \tau_0$; the printed $\mathcal{T}(Y_i, Z_i)$ and the corrected $\mathcal{T}(\tilde y_{i,Z_i=0}, Z_i)$ agree for this statistic if and only if $\tau_0 = 0$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Potential outcomes and observed outcome: p. 396 (PDF p. 2)] “Say $Y_i$ is the observed outcome, and we hypothesize that units do not interfere and also that $y_{i,Z_i=1} = y_{i,Z_i=0} + \tau$”; “the identity $Y_i = Z_i y_{i,Z_i=1} + (1 - Z_i) y_{i,Z_i=0}$”. [Adjusted outcome: step (2)] $\tilde y_{i,Z_i=0} = Y_i - Z_i\tau_0$. [Test statistic and reference distribution: step (3)] “a test statistic, $\mathcal{T}(\tilde y_{i,Z_i=0}, Z_i)$. A distribution of values for this test statistic arises from repetitions of the treatment assignment process (new draws of $\mathbf{z}$ from all of the ways that such treatment assignment vectors could have been produced)”. [The $p$ value: step (4)] “a $p$ value arises by comparing the observed test statistic, $\mathcal{T}(Y_i, Z_i)$ against the distribution of that test statistic that characterizes the hypothesis”; no formula or tail is printed.
canonical_claim.note: Corrected statement for a Minor error (a misprinted symbol in the description of the procedure), included on the author's instruction that every confirmed mathematical error has a corrected-statement target. Repair as settled in validated.json (sol.smallest_repair; prior_correction.status ‘correct’); repair cost: none. (a) and the identity in (c) are the validator's derivation (first paragraph: ‘$u_i = Y_i - \tau_0 Z_i$ equals the fixed control potential outcome $y_i(0)$’ and ‘For a difference in means, $T(Y,Z) = T(u,Z) + \tau_0$’); (b) is the conclusion the procedure needs and is proved in general form under P016-T12. The correction changes no computation: the released code already uses the adjusted outcomes on both sides.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The three displayed definitions of the test statistics as printed: the KS formula of footnote 3 (no absolute value), equation (1) (mean not specified) and equation (2) (no row index; no intercept listed); the witnesses are the validator's constructions and are not in the paper
canonical_claim.location: footnote 3, p. 396 (PDF p. 2); equation (1), p. 397 (PDF p. 3); equation (2) and the sentence before it, p. 399 (PDF p. 5)
canonical_claim.statement:
Exact witnesses (the validator's; not in the paper) that the three displays, read literally, do not define the statistics that the surrounding text describes and the released code computes. Notation as in standing assumption (S9).
(i) [Footnote 3 without absolute values is a different, one-sided statistic] For $u = (0,1,2,3)$ and $z = (0,0,1,1)$ (controls $0,1$; treated $2,3$), the differences $F_1(t) - F_0(t)$ at $t = 0,1,2,3$ are $-\tfrac12, -1, -\tfrac12, 0$. The printed statistic $\max_i[F_1(u_i) - F_0(u_i)]$ equals $0$; the two-sided statistic $\max_i|F_1(u_i) - F_0(u_i)|$ equals $1$. With the labels exchanged, $z = (1,1,0,0)$, the printed statistic equals $1$ and the two-sided statistic is again $1$.
(ii) [Equation (1) with the pooled mean does not depend on the assignment] If the bar in equation (1) is read as the mean over all units, $\bar u = n^{-1}\sum_i u_i$, the display is $\sum_i (u_i - \bar u)^2$, which is the same number for every assignment $z$; its randomization distribution is a point mass, and every inclusive-tail randomization $p$ value equals $1$ for every hypothesis. For $u = (0,1,2,3)$ this number is $5$ under all six assignments with two treated units, whereas the residual sum of squares on an intercept and $z$ is $R(u,z) = 1,4,5,5,4,1$ on the treated sets $\{1,2\},\{1,3\},\{1,4\},\{2,3\},\{2,4\},\{3,4\}$; at the treated set $\{1,2\}$ the lower-tail $p$ value $\Pr\{R(u,Z) \le R(u,z)\}$ is $\tfrac13$ and the pooled-mean statistic's is $1$.
(iii) [Equation (2) with the listed regressors only, without an intercept, is a different statistic] Six units; the only edge is $\{1,2\}$; $z = (1,0,1,0,1,0)$; $u = (1,1,1,1,1,1)$. The design matrix with rows $(1, z_i, (z^TS)_i, (1^TS)_i)$ is $$X = \begin{pmatrix} 1&1&0&1\\ 1&0&1&1\\ 1&1&0&0\\ 1&0&0&0\\ 1&1&0&0\\ 1&0&0&0 \end{pmatrix}.$$ The least-squares residual sum of squares of $u$ on these four columns is $0$ (coefficients $(1,0,0,0)$). On the three listed columns $(z_i, (z^TS)_i, (1^TS)_i)$ alone it is $2$ (coefficients $(1,1,0)$; rows 4 and 6 are zero rows and each leaves residual $1$).
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [KS as printed: footnote 3, p. 396 (PDF p. 2)] “the KS test statistic is $\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{y}_0, \mathbf{z})_{\mathrm{KS}} = \max_{i=1,\ldots,n}[F_1(y_{i,0}) - F_0(y_{i,0})]$, where $F(x) = (1/n)\sum_{i=1}^{n} I(x_i \le x)$”. [Equation (1) as printed: p. 397 (PDF p. 3)] $\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{y}_0, \mathbf{z})_{\mathrm{SSR}} \equiv \sum_i (\tilde y_{i,Z_i=0} - \bar{\tilde y}_{i,Z_i=0})^2$, introduced as summing “the difference between the mean of the outcome implied by the hypothesis and individual outcomes”. [Equation (2) as printed: p. 399 (PDF p. 5)] “If we collected $Z_i$, $\mathbf{z}^T\mathbf{S}$, and $\mathbf{1}^T\mathbf{S}$ into a matrix $\mathbf{X}$, and fit the $\tilde y_{i,Z_i=0}$ as a linear function of $\mathbf{X}$ with fitted coefficients $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ then we could define the test statistic as $\mathcal{T}(y_0, \mathbf{z})_{\mathrm{SSR}} \equiv \sum_i (\tilde y_{i,Z_i=0} - \mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})^2$.” In the display the summand subtracts the whole vector $\mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ from the scalar $\tilde y_{i,Z_i=0}$. [Adjacency matrix: p. 399] $\mathbf{S}$ is the “fixed binary adjacency matrix”; in (iii) $(z^TS)_i$ is the number of treated neighbours of $i$ and $(1^TS)_i$ its degree.
canonical_claim.note: P016-E002 is rated an error, Minor (misprints in three displayed definitions), so priority 3. Sol's verdict: confirmed_in_part (upheld on re-run), evidence type exact_counterexample; false as printed, not false under the natural reading (the regression text and the released code fix the intended statistics, and every reported computation uses them). Limits recorded by Sol and kept here: (ii) is conditional on reading the undefined bar as the pooled mean, which the paper does not say; (iii) is conditional on reading the regressor list as exhaustive, and an unstated intercept is not by itself an error; the signed maximum in (i) is a valid one-sided statistic, and the defect is that it is not the two-sided statistic described and used. (i) is section 2, (ii) section 3 and (iii) section 4 of the validator's derivation.md (exact_output.txt in the same folder); all numbers were recomputed for this list. The type mismatch in the summand of equation (2) (a scalar minus an $n$-vector) is a defect of the display and has no witness of its own.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Footnote 3 and equations (1) and (2), corrected: the two-sided KS distance, the group-mean residual sum of squares and the indexed least-squares residual sum of squares with an intercept
canonical_claim.location: footnote 3, p. 396 (PDF p. 2); equation (1), p. 397 (PDF p. 3); equation (2) and the sentence before it, p. 399 (PDF p. 5)
canonical_claim.statement:
Sol's repair (validated.json, P016-E002, smallest_repair), verbatim: “Let u_i=\tilde y_{i,Z_i=0}, n_g=\#\{i:z_i=g\}>0, and \bar u_g=n_g^{-1}\sum_{i:z_i=g}u_i. Replace equation (1) by R(u,z)=\sum_i(u_i-\bar u_{z_i})^2 and say "sums the squared differences from the respective assignment-group means." In equation (2), use R_X(u,z)=\min_b\|u-X(z)b\|_2^2=\sum_i\{u_i-(X(z)\hat b)_i\}^2; explicitly include the conventional intercept. For section 2.1 use x_i^T=(1,z_i,(z^T S)_i,(1^T S)_i). In footnote 3 restore absolute values: D=\max_i|F_1(u_i)-F_0(u_i)|=\sup_t|F_1(t)-F_0(t)|. For clarity one can define F_g(t)=n_g^{-1}\sum_{i:z_i=g}I(u_i\le t).”
Corrected displays. [Footnote 3] $\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{y}_0, \mathbf{z})_{\mathrm{KS}} = \max_{i=1,\ldots,n}\left|F_1(u_i) - F_0(u_i)\right|$ with $F_g(t) = n_g^{-1}\sum_{i: z_i = g} I(u_i \le t)$. [Equation (1)] $\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{y}_0, \mathbf{z})_{\mathrm{SSR}} \equiv \sum_i (u_i - \bar u_{z_i})^2$ with $\bar u_g = n_g^{-1}\sum_{i: z_i = g} u_i$, which “sums the squared differences from the respective assignment-group means”. [Equation (2)] $\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{y}_0, \mathbf{z})_{\mathrm{SSR}} \equiv \sum_i \{u_i - (\mathbf{X}(z)\hat b)_i\}^2 = \min_b \|u - \mathbf{X}(z) b\|_2^2$, where $\mathbf{X}(z)$ has rows $x_i^T = (1, z_i, (z^TS)_i, (1^TS)_i)$. Here $u_i = \tilde y_{i,Z_i=0}$.
Mathematical content, with every hypothesis. Let $u \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $z \in \{0,1\}^n$ with $n_0, n_1 > 0$.
(a) [Equation (1) is the regression residual sum of squares] $\sum_i (u_i - \bar u_{z_i})^2 = \min_{(a,b) \in \mathbb{R}^2}\sum_i (u_i - a - bz_i)^2$, the minimum being attained exactly at $a = \bar u_0$, $b = \bar u_1 - \bar u_0$.
(b) [Equation (2) is well defined] For every real $n \times k$ matrix $X$ the minimum $R_X(u) = \min_{b \in \mathbb{R}^k}\|u - Xb\|_2^2$ is attained; for every minimizer $\hat b$ the fitted vector $X\hat b$ is the same, and $\sum_i \{u_i - (X\hat b)_i\}^2 = R_X(u)$. No full-rank condition on $X$ is needed. If $X$ has the two columns $\mathbf{1}$ and $z$, then $R_X(u)$ is the statistic of (a).
(c) [The maximum over the sample points is the supremum over all thresholds] $\max_{1 \le i \le n}|F_1(u_i) - F_0(u_i)| = \sup_{t \in \mathbb{R}}|F_1(t) - F_0(t)|$, also when $u$ has ties; this statistic is unchanged when the labels of the two groups are exchanged and lies in $[0,1]$.
(d) [Rows of the design in Section 2.1] For a symmetric adjacency matrix $S$, $(z^TS)_i = \sum_j S_{ij}z_j$ (the number of treated neighbours of $i$) and $(1^TS)_i = \sum_j S_{ij}$ (the degree of $i$).
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [As printed] footnote 3 (p. 396), equation (1) (p. 397) and equation (2) with its introducing sentence (p. 399), transcribed under P016-T9 and in standing assumptions (S3), (S5), (S6). [The statistics the text describes] p. 399: “the SSRs from a least squares regression of $\tilde y_{i,Z_i=0}$ on $Z_i$ and $\mathbf{z}^T\mathbf{S}$ (i.e., the number of directly connected nodes assigned treatment) as well as the $\mathbf{1}^T\mathbf{S}$ (i.e., the degree of the node)”; p. 400: “the third version (SSR) includes only treatment assignment $\mathbf{z}$”; p. 402: “SSR from an ordinary least squares regression”; p. 396: the KS statistic is used “so that their tests would be sensitive to differences in the treatment and control distributions implied by different hypotheses and not only sensitive to differences in one aspect of those distributions”. [Network: p. 399] $\mathbf{S}$ is the fixed binary adjacency matrix; the BFP network is undirected, so $S$ is symmetric.
canonical_claim.note: Corrected statement for a Minor error (misprints in three displayed formulas), included on the author's instruction that every confirmed mathematical error has a corrected-statement target. Repair as settled in validated.json (sol.smallest_repair, identical to prior_correction.corrected_text, status ‘correct’); repair cost: none, since the released functions already compute these statistics. The corrections are to definitions, so there is no theorem of the paper to restate; (a)–(d) are the exact facts that make the corrected displays well defined and equal to what the text describes ((a) is section 3 of the validator's derivation.md, (b) and (d) section 4, (c) section 2). The paper does not use the word ‘two-sided’; the absolute value restores the usual KS distance that the passage describes and the code computes. The explicit intercept is the conventional one; Sol does not treat its omission from the prose list as proof of a wrong regression.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 1, ‘test statistics with this property (“effect increasing” test statistics)’, which identifies a statistic that is small for similar and large for divergent distributions with an effect increasing statistic, as printed; the witnesses are the validator's constructions and are not in the paper
canonical_claim.location: pp. 396–397 (PDF pp. 2–3): the quotation that runs from the last line of p. 396 to the first lines of p. 397, and the sentence after it
canonical_claim.statement:
Exact witnesses (the validator's; not in the paper) that a statistic that is small when the treated and control distributions are similar and large when they diverge need not be effect increasing. Definition (the validator's statement of the property; the paper does not define it): a statistic $T(y,z)$ is effect increasing if, for every fixed assignment $z$ and all outcome vectors $y, y'$ with $y'_i \ge y_i$ whenever $z_i = 1$ and $y'_i \le y_i$ whenever $z_i = 0$, one has $T(y',z) \ge T(y,z)$. $D(y,z) = \max_i|F_1(y_i) - F_0(y_i)|$ is the two-sided KS distance, which is $0$ when the two empirical distributions coincide and $1$ when their supports are separated.
(i) Let $z = (1,1,0,0)$, $y = (0,1,2,3)$ and $y' = (2,3,2,3)$. Both treated responses rise by $2$ and both control responses are unchanged. For $y$ the differences $F_1 - F_0$ at $0,1,2,3$ are $\tfrac12, 1, \tfrac12, 0$, so $D(y,z) = 1$; for $y'$ both groups have the values $\{2,3\}$, so $D(y',z) = 0$. Thus $D(y',z) < D(y,z)$: the two-sided KS distance is not effect increasing. The signed maximum printed in footnote 3, $\max_i[F_1(y_i) - F_0(y_i)]$, also falls from $1$ to $0$.
(ii) With strict changes in both groups: $z = (1,1,0,0)$, $y = (0,1,4,5)$, $y' = (2,3,2,3)$; both treated responses rise, both control responses fall, and $D$ falls from $1$ to $0$.
(iii) [The residual sum of squares is not effect increasing in either orientation] Let $z = (1,1,0,0)$ and $y = (0,2,0,2)$, so $R(y,z) = 4$. Raising the first treated response to $1$ gives $R((1,2,0,2),z) = \tfrac52 < 4$; raising the second treated response to $3$ gives $R((0,3,0,2),z) = \tfrac{13}{2} > 4$. So neither $R$ nor $-R$ is effect increasing.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [As printed: pp. 396–397 (PDF pp. 2–3)] “BFP repeat his general advice: “Select a test statistic [$\mathcal{T}$] that will be small when the treated and control distributions in the adjusted data . . . are similar, and large when the distributions diverge.” Rosenbaum (2002, Proposition 4 and 5, section 2.9) presents results proving that test statistics with this property (“effect increasing” test statistics) produce an unbiased test of the hypothesis of no effects or positive effects when the positive effects involve one parameter.” The paper gives no definition of ‘effect increasing’; the definition above is the directional monotonicity condition labelled (EI) in the validator's derivation and in Sol's repair. [KS: footnote 3, p. 396] as in standing assumption (S3). [$R$] the residual sum of squares on an intercept and $z$, standing assumption (S9).
